title: Six animals
hookLine: a snake, crocodile, bird, dog, jackal and monkey tied to one post: the body as the post (SN 35.247)

cards: A man walks into a clearing with six animals on six ropes. A snake. A crocodile.
A bird. A dog. A jackal.
A monkey. He knots the six ropes together in the middle, and lets go. The snake heads for its anthill.

The crocodile for the river. The bird for the sky, the dog for the village, the jackal for the charnel ground, the monkey for the forest. Six directions, one knot, and whoever is strongest drags the rest.

teach.b: The story comes from the Connected Discourses, in the book on the six senses, and the Buddha tells it twice.

teach.h: THE SAME ANIMALS, TIED TO A POST.
teach.b: The first time, the ropes are only tied to each other, and the others get dragged after whichever animal is strongest. Then he tells it again with a single change.
The man ties all six ropes to a strong post, driven deep into the ground. The animals pull just as hard. The snake still wants its anthill.
The monkey still wants its forest. Nobody has been tamed. But the post doesn't move.
After a while, worn out, they stand by the post, then sit down by it, then lie down beside it.
The six animals are the six senses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, each pulling toward what it likes and away from what it doesn't.

teach.h: THE POST: MINDFULNESS OF THE BODY.
teach.b: The post is mindfulness directed to the body, kayagata sati: knowing you're sitting while you sit, breathing while you breathe. The Buddha doesn't say kill the animals, or blindfold the eye. The senses keep their nature.
What changes is that there's something steady to be tied to. Under right mindfulness, the seventh factor of the path, mindfulness isn't a mood.
It's a post. Some teachers put it this way: the body is always here; it's the mind that runs off to the anthill and the forest.
And that ends a week: waking the good, keeping it going, the lute string, remembering to notice, the gatekeeper, the bowl of oil, and six animals with something to be tied to.

how: Many Buddhists practice mindfulness of the body by returning attention to posture and breath through the day, in walking as well as sitting meditation; teachers in several schools describe the body as an anchor for the wandering mind.

o: six wild urges a monk has to kill off
the six senses, each pulling its own way
six rebirths a being passes through

games.q: match each animal to where it pulls, or what it stands for.

s: in the story, the Buddha says to get rid of the six animals
the animals keep their nature; tied to a post, they pull until they tire and lie down.
the six animals stand for the six senses, including the mind
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind: each pulls toward its own range.
tied only to each other, the animals end up following the strongest
that's the first telling; the second adds the post.

games.q: you've tied six animals to a strong post driven deep into the ground. they pull in six directions. what happens, in the Buddha's story?
o: they pull, tire, and lie down beside the post
the strongest drags the others away
games.why: the post doesn't move. worn out, the animals stand, then sit, then lie down beside it. the senses aren't destroyed; they're given something steady.

practice: Find the post first: your feet, the weight of your body on the seat, your hands where they rest.

Then let the animals pull, a sound, a thought about tomorrow, an itch, and each time, notice which one is pulling and come back to the weight of the body; coming back to the feet on the floor is coming back to the post.

wordCard.voice: Six animals. The six senses, each pulling toward its own place, tied to one steady post: mindfulness of the body.

orig.note: Pali saḷāyatana: the six sense bases, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, which the six animals stand for.

carryVoice: Your line: the post holds. The animals keep their nature, and the post doesn't move. A week done: day three hundred ninety-two.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 35.247 (Chappana Sutta, the simile of the six animals)
Majjhima Nikaya 119, Kayagatasati Sutta (mindfulness of the body)
